newsitem.title: USA: Fed nominee Ferguson to bring banking expertise.
newsitem.headline: Fed nominee Ferguson to bring banking expertise.

text.p: Roger Ferguson Jr., nominated by President Bill Clinton to the Federal Reserve Board on Thursday, is regarded as a realist who will bring much-needed expertise in banking.

If confirmed by the Senate, Ferguson, a partner at the New York-based international consulting firm McKinsey and Co. Inc., would be only the third black to serve on the seven-member board in its history.
Ferguson began working for McKinsey as a consultant in 1984 specialising in management strategies, including the increasingly deregulated U.S. banking industry.
"The Fed has been looking for someone with an expertise in banking for a long time, in fact, since (Fed Governor John) LaWare left," a source close to the Fed said.
"It's particularly important for the Fed to have a banker at this juncture due to new regulations and technology-driven changes in the industry," the source added.
As one of the key regulators of U.S. banks, the Fed has found it difficult in the past to attract bankers due to potential conflicts of interest.
LaWare, the last bank expert at the board, left in 1995 and was replaced by economist Laurence Meyer.

"The Fed will find in Roger Ferguson somebody who is very knowledgeable about banking and also very good at problem-solving. The Fed is dealing with rather complex problems," a McKinsey executive said in an interview, referring to the role of the Fed in the U.S. payments system.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan last year appointed a special commission, headed by Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin, to look into the role the Fed should play in providing financial services to a banking industry that is rapidly evolving due to new regulations and advanced technology.
"Ferguson was trained as a consultant to deal with those kind of problems," the McKinsey executive added. "And he is a wonderful academic."

Ferguson earned a Ph.D. in economics from Harvard University and wrote his dissertation on joint ventures in the manufacturing sector. He also holds a law degree from Harvard and practiced as an attorney with the firm of Davis Polk & Wardwell, specialising in corporate mergers and public offerings.
McKinsey, a firm with 600 partners and 3,400 consultants in 39 countries, said Ferguson, as director of research and information, also played a role in the company's strategy.

Born in Washington, Ferguson is the son of an Army map-maker and a schoolteacher. The Fed has come under criticism by civil rights advocates for insufficient minority representation, a record that Clinton vowed to improve.

The two other blacks to have served as Fed governors were Emmett Rice, appointed by President Jimmy Carter and Andrew Brimmer, appointed by President Lyndon Johnson. Rice was Fed governor from 1979 to 1986 and Brimmer from 1966 to 1974.
Clinton last year named Rivlin as the first woman vice chair of the Fed, bringing to an unprecedented three the number of women sitting simultaneously on the board.
